planting.note: Pot up offsets or rooted leaf cuttings in spring into a mineral, fast-draining succulent mix; like other soft-leaved Haworthia, this species tolerates more shade than typical succulents and should never sit in hot direct sun.

directions: Native to the hills around Graaff-Reinet in South Africa's Eastern Cape, this stemless rosette curls its pale green, longitudinally lined leaves inward and edges them with fine, hairlike white bristles that give the whole plant a cobwebbed, spider-like look. Because it naturally grows tucked among rocks and low scrub, it prefers bright but filtered light or partial shade rather than the intense sun many other succulents demand, and the bristles themselves help diffuse harsh light. Water only once the gritty mix has dried out fully, and let clumps form naturally from basal offsets rather than forcing division. Slender flower stalks up to 20 inches tall carry small white, brown-veined blooms in late spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a lean, fast-draining mineral mix in bright, filtered light; this slow-growing species resents being disturbed, so repot only when a clump has clearly outgrown its container.

directions: Found on quartzitic rock in the Rooiberg range southeast of Calitzdorp in South Africa's Western Cape, this unusual species departs from the typical Haworthia rosette, instead producing slender, channeled, grass-like leaves up to 16 inches long from thick, fusiform storage roots. It is notably slow-growing and, in its native quartz fields, is shaded for part of the day by surrounding rock and vegetation, so filtered light or partial shade suits it better than full sun in cultivation. Keep in a very lean, mineral succulent mix and water sparingly, allowing the substrate to dry completely between waterings to protect the thick roots from rot. Small white, brown-veined flowers appear in loose spirals on slim stalks.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Pot in a fast-draining succulent mix and place in bright indirect light or partial shade; water on a winter-active rhythm since this Cederberg native often grows with other winter-rainfall succulents.

directions: Native to the Cederberg and surrounding Northern Cape foothills of South Africa, this compact species forms stemless rosettes of thick, fleshy, pale to purplish-green leaves marked with translucent spotting and edged with short, soft spines along the keel and margins. In its winter-rainfall habitat it is often tucked beneath shrubs or rock overhangs, so it grows best indoors or outdoors in bright filtered light or partial shade rather than harsh midday sun, which can bronze or scorch the leaf faces. Let the mineral-rich, fast-draining mix dry out completely between waterings, tapering off further during the summer dormant period. Several named varieties exist, differing mainly in flower shape and leaf spotting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in a fast-draining succulent mix in bright indirect light or partial shade; brighter conditions bring out the leaf coloring, but this species still tolerates more shade than most true cacti and stem succulents.

directions: Native to the Steytlerville area of South Africa's Eastern Cape, this slow-growing species was long treated as Haworthia venosa subsp. woolleyi before being placed in the hard-leaved genus Haworthiopsis. It forms small, solitary to slowly clustering rosettes of triangular, dark green to brownish leaves marked with fine vertical lines on the upper surface and small raised tubercles and white marginal teeth on the underside. Although Haworthiopsis species generally tolerate more sun than soft-leaved Haworthia, this one still colors and grows best in semi-shaded, filtered light rather than harsh exposure. Water only once the fast-draining mineral mix is fully dry, and expect a long raceme of small white flowers from spring into fall.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
